# Packet switching and computer networks (`packet_switching_networks`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: needs programmable_computer; helped by sampling_pcm, error_correcting_codes, information_theory, operating_system_time_sharing
- Core idea: Instead of reserving a whole line between two parties for the length of a call, cut every message into short blocks (packets), each carrying information that lets the network forward it. Small computers at the junctions of the network pass each packet on using routing tables. Where reliable ordered delivery is needed, a transport protocol can number the data, detect gaps and arrange retransmission. Lines are then shared efficiently by many bursty users, and the network keeps working when links or junctions fail, because packets flow round the damage. Networks of different kinds are joined by an agreed common packet format and addressing scheme, with reliability left to the computers at the two ends.
- Pitfalls:
  - A central exchange through which everything must pass; it is a single point of failure and a bottleneck
  - Demanding that the network itself never loses a packet; simple junctions and checking at the ends work better
  - Saying the ARPANET was built to survive nuclear war; that was Baran's motive at RAND, the ARPANET was built to share scarce computers
  - No thought for trust: the early protocols assumed friendly users, and security had to be added painfully later
- History: americas: 1960–1964 – Baran's studies of distributed networks at RAND; 1961–1964 Kleinrock's queueing theory of message networks; October 1969 first ARPANET link; 1973 Ethernet (Metcalfe, Xerox); 1974 Cerf and Kahn publish their internetwork protocol. The later TCP and IP protocols replace NCP on the ARPANET in January 1983; europe: 1965–1966 – Donald Davies at the National Physical Laboratory designs the same scheme independently and coins 'packet'; 1972–1973 Pouzin's CYCLADES network (France) puts reliability in the end computers; 1989–1991 World Wide Web (Berners-Lee, CERN)
- Read:
  - Vinton G. Cerf & Robert E. Kahn, A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication, IEEE Transactions on Communications 22 (1974)
  - Janet Abbate, Inventing the Internet (1999)
